text:
The 2026 US-Iran military escalation stemmed from years of heightened tensions surrounding Iran's nuclear program, its development of ballistic missiles, and its expanding military influence across the Middle East. Attempts to renegotiate a nuclear deal in 2025 and 2026 proved unsuccessful, further exacerbating the situation. A brutal crackdown on widespread Iranian protests in late 2025 and early 2026, which reportedly killed thousands of demonstrators, also contributed to the deteriorating relationship, prompting the United States to undertake its largest military buildup in the Middle East since 2003.

Hostilities formally erupted on February 28, 2026, when the United States, in coordination with Israel, launched a series of military operations against Iran. These initial strikes targeted Iranian military infrastructure, air defenses, and leadership, notably resulting in the death of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei. Iran swiftly retaliated with extensive missile and drone attacks against US military assets and allied nations throughout the Middle East, including facilities in Jordan, Kuwait, and Bahrain, and by blocking the Strait of Hormuz.

As of July 2026, the conflict remains ongoing, characterized by a cycle of strikes and counter-strikes despite several attempts at ceasefires. The US has continued to target Iranian military infrastructure, including air defenses and missile sites, while Iran has responded with attacks on commercial vessels and regional US allies, leading to warnings about Tehran's control over the Strait of Hormuz. The war has incurred significant human and economic costs, with global energy markets experiencing volatility and the US alone estimating the cost of the war at over $113 billion by June 2026. Diplomatic efforts persist, though a lasting resolution has yet to be achieved.
